title: Oscillations and circular motion: practice questions (AI-written)

questions.question: A particle of constant mass moves in a horizontal circle at constant angular velocity. The radius of the circle and the angular velocity are both doubled. By what factor does the centripetal force on the particle change? A 2, B 4, C 8, D 16
steps: F = m omega^2 r. Doubling omega increases F by a factor of 2^2 = 4, and doubling r increases it by a further factor of 2.
The total factor is 4 x 2 = 8, option C.
A allows only for the change in r, B only for the change in omega, and D squares the radius as well as the angular velocity.

questions.question: A puck of mass 0.20 kg is attached to a string of length 0.50 m, fixed at the other end, and moves in a horizontal circle on a smooth table with an angular velocity of 4.0 rad s^-1. What is the tension in the string? A 0.40 N, B 0.80 N, C 1.6 N, D 3.2 N
steps: The tension is the only horizontal force and provides the centripetal force: T = m omega^2 r.
A uses m omega r, B uses m omega^2 r^2, and D uses twice the radius.

questions.question: Define the radian.
questions.answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius of the circle.
steps: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius
accept: Angle in radians = arc length / radius
The angle for which arc length = radius, with 2 pi radians in a full circle

questions.question: The Moon moves in a circular orbit about the Earth of radius 3.84 x 10^8 m. The orbital period is 27.3 days. Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the Moon.
questions.answer: a = 2.7 x 10^-3 m s^-2 towards the Earth.
steps: Angular velocity omega = 2 pi / T = 2.66 x 10^-6 rad s^-1.
a = omega^2 r = (2.66 x 10^-6)^2 x 3.84 x 10^8 = 2.72 x 10^-3 m s^-2, directed towards the Earth.

questions.question: A car travels round a bend in a flat road at constant speed. Explain why the car is more likely to skid if the road is wet.
questions.answer: Friction provides the centripetal force; the maximum friction is lower when wet, so the car skids at a lower speed.
steps: On a flat road the sideways friction between the tyres and the road provides the centripetal force m v^2 / r
The maximum friction available is smaller when the road is wet
If m v^2 / r exceeds this maximum the tyres cannot keep the car on the circle, so it skids (at a lower speed on a wet road)
accept: The coefficient of friction between tyre and road is lower when wet
Water forms a film between tyre and road, reducing grip
The centripetal force needed is proportional to v^2, so a small increase in speed greatly increases the friction required
The car skids outwards, moving along a straighter path (tangent) rather than round the bend

questions.question: A pilot of mass 72 kg flies an aircraft in a vertical circular loop of radius 450 m at a constant speed of 85 m s^-1. State the direction of the resultant force on the pilot at the lowest point and at the highest point of the loop.
questions.answer: At the lowest point the resultant force is vertically upwards; at the highest point it is vertically downwards (towards the centre of the circle each time).
steps: At the lowest point the resultant force is vertically upwards (towards the centre of the circle)
At the highest point the resultant force is vertically downwards (towards the centre of the circle)
accept: The resultant force always acts towards the centre of the circle because the speed is constant
The resultant force is the centripetal force of magnitude m v^2 / r at both points
The resultant force is perpendicular to the velocity at every point

questions.question: The pilot (mass 72 kg) flies a vertical loop of radius 450 m at a constant speed of 85 m s^-1. Calculate the force exerted by the seat on the pilot at the lowest point of the loop.
questions.answer: R = 1.86 x 10^3 N (about 1.9 x 10^3 N), directed upwards.
steps: Centripetal acceleration v^2 / r = 85^2 / 450 = 16.06 m s^-2.
At the lowest point the seat force R acts upwards and the weight mg downwards: R - mg = m v^2 / r.

questions.question: Calculate the force exerted by the seat on the pilot at the highest point of the same loop (pilot mass 72 kg, radius 450 m, speed 85 m s^-1).
steps: At the highest point both the weight mg and the seat force R act downwards (towards the centre): R + mg = m v^2 / r.
The seat force is much smaller than at the lowest point, because the weight now helps to provide the centripetal force.

questions.question: The pilot of mass 72 kg now flies the loop of radius 450 m more slowly. Determine the minimum speed at the highest point at which the pilot stays in contact with the seat.
steps: At the minimum speed the seat force falls to zero, so the weight alone provides the centripetal force.
m g = m v^2 / r, so v = sqrt(g r).

questions.question: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.12 m and frequency 2.5 Hz. What is the maximum acceleration of the object? A 0.75 m s^-2, B 1.9 m s^-2, C 4.7 m s^-2, D 30 m s^-2
steps: Angular frequency omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 2.5 = 15.71 rad s^-1.
a_max = omega^2 A = 15.71^2 x 0.12 = 29.6 m s^-2, option D.
A uses omega = f, B is the maximum speed omega A, and C forgets to square the factor 2 pi.

questions.question: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude A. When its displacement from the equilibrium position is A/2, what fraction of its total energy is kinetic energy? A 3/4, B 1/4, C 1/2, D sqrt(3)/2
steps: Potential energy is proportional to x^2, so at x = A/2 the potential energy is (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of the total energy.
The total energy is constant, so the kinetic energy is 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 of the total, option A.
B is the potential energy fraction, C assumes equal sharing, and D is the ratio of the speed to the maximum speed, not of the energies.

questions.question: Explain why the motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic only for small angular displacements.
questions.answer: The restoring force is mg sin(theta), which is proportional to the displacement only when sin(theta) is approximately equal to theta (small angles in radians).
steps: The restoring force is the component of the weight along the arc, F = -mg sin(theta)
For small angles sin(theta) is approximately theta (in radians), and the displacement along the arc is x = l theta, so F = -(mg / l) x
The force (and the acceleration) is then proportional to the displacement and in the opposite direction, which is the condition for SHM; for large angles sin(theta) is not proportional to theta
accept: a = -(g / l) x is of the form a = -omega^2 x with omega^2 = g / l
The period T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g) is independent of amplitude only for small angles
For large angles the restoring force increases less than proportionally to displacement, so the period increases

questions.question: A mass of 0.35 kg hangs from a vertical spring of spring constant 28 N m^-1. The mass is pulled down 4.5 cm from its equilibrium position and released, and it oscillates with simple harmonic motion. Calculate (i) the period of the oscillation and (ii) the maximum speed of the mass.
questions.answer: (i) T = 0.70 s; (ii) maximum speed = 0.40 m s^-1.
steps: (i) T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k) = 2 pi sqrt(0.35 / 28).
T = 0.702 s, which is 0.70 s.
(ii) The amplitude is the initial displacement, A = 0.045 m, and omega = sqrt(k / m) = sqrt(28 / 0.35) = 8.944 rad s^-1.
v_max = omega A = 8.944 x 0.045 = 0.402 m s^-1, which is 0.40 m s^-1.

questions.question: A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 8.0 cm and frequency 1.5 Hz. At time t = 0 it is at its maximum positive displacement. Calculate the displacement of the particle at t = 0.20 s.
questions.answer: x = -2.5 cm (on the opposite side of equilibrium from the starting position).
steps: Starting at maximum displacement, x = A cos(omega t) with omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 1.5 = 9.425 rad s^-1.
omega t = 9.425 x 0.20 = 1.885 rad (calculator in radian mode).
x = 8.0 cos(1.885) = -2.47 cm, so the displacement is -2.5 cm.

questions.question: A mass of 0.40 kg hangs from a vertical spring and oscillates vertically with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 5.0 cm and frequency 1.6 Hz. Calculate the maximum acceleration of the mass.
steps: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 1.6 = 10.05 rad s^-1.
The maximum acceleration is at maximum displacement: a_max = omega^2 A.

questions.question: The mass of 0.40 kg oscillates with amplitude 5.0 cm and frequency 1.6 Hz. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation.
steps: Total energy = maximum kinetic energy = (1/2) m v_max^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.

questions.question: Using the total energy of 0.0505 J from (b)(i), calculate the kinetic energy of the mass when its displacement from equilibrium is 3.0 cm. The amplitude is 5.0 cm.
steps: The potential energy of the oscillation at displacement x is E x^2 / A^2, and the kinetic energy is the total energy minus this.
KE = 0.032 J. (Check: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = 0.402 m s^-1 and (1/2) m v^2 = 0.032 J.)

questions.question: The mass is now made to oscillate while it is fully immersed in oil, which gives light damping. Describe and explain how the amplitude and the period of the oscillations change.
questions.answer: The amplitude decreases with each oscillation because the oil does work against the motion and removes energy; the period stays approximately the same for light damping.
steps: The oil exerts a resistive (drag) force that opposes the motion, so the system does work against it and loses energy (as thermal energy in the oil)
The total energy falls on each cycle, so the amplitude decreases with time (exponentially for light damping)
For light damping the period (frequency) is almost unchanged
accept: The amplitude decreases by the same fraction each cycle
Energy of oscillation is proportional to amplitude squared, so the energy falls as the amplitude falls
If the damping is not removed the oscillations eventually die away completely
Greater damping would give a slightly longer period, up to critical damping where there are no oscillations

questions.question: The upper end of the spring is now moved up and down by a motor, which drives the system at a frequency that can be varied. The natural frequency of the undamped system is 1.6 Hz. Describe how the amplitude of the mass changes as the driving frequency is increased from well below to well above 1.6 Hz, and state the effect of increased damping on the response.
questions.answer: Amplitude peaks at 1.6 Hz (resonance) and is small either side; more damping lowers and broadens the peak.
steps: At driving frequencies well below 1.6 Hz the amplitude is small
As the driving frequency approaches the natural frequency of 1.6 Hz the amplitude increases to a maximum (resonance)
Above the natural frequency the amplitude falls again
Greater damping reduces the maximum amplitude and makes the resonance peak broader (less sharp)
accept: At resonance the driving frequency equals the natural frequency and energy is transferred most efficiently to the oscillator
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system
With very light damping the amplitude at resonance becomes very large
At very high driving frequencies the mass hardly moves, so the amplitude is small
